topic: How Do Submarines Make Unlimited Air Underwater?
angle: Over 140 sailors can live locked in an airtight steel tube deep underwater for four months without ever suffocating, because the submarine continuously synthesizes breathable air from the ocean.
why: Explainer videos on extreme closed-system engineering regularly pull tens of millions of views (e.g. 18.5M on underwater tunnel engineering, 16.6M on jet engine mechanics, and 35.1M on underwater hydrostatic pressure). This question taps into a universal claustrophobic mystery that nearly everyone has wondered about, answered through clean, step-by-step physics and chemistry.
keywords: how do nuclear submarines get air
how long can a submarine stay submerged
facts: Modern nuclear submarines routinely stay submerged hundreds of meters deep for 90 to 120 consecutive days without surfacing.
A typical military submarine crew of 130 to 160 sailors consumes roughly 20 to 25 cubic meters of pure oxygen every 24 hours.
Submarines do not carry thousands of heavy compressed oxygen tanks because high-pressure tanks take up massive cargo space and present severe explosion risks.
Instead, the submarine manufactures fresh oxygen continuously on demand using an onboard life-support system called an Oxygen Generator Plant (OGP).
Seawater is brought into the hull and purified through multi-stage distillation or reverse osmosis to remove all salts and impurities, yielding deionized water.
The ultra-pure water is pumped into an electrolysis unit powered by the vessel's nuclear reactor, which provides virtually unlimited electrical power.
High-amperage electrical current passes between electrodes in the water, splitting liquid H2O molecules into gaseous oxygen (O2) and hydrogen (H2).
The pure oxygen gas is regulated and pumped directly into the submarine's central air ducts to maintain atmospheric oxygen between 18% and 21%.
Hydrogen gas is highly explosive, so it is immediately compressed and pumped out through the hull to dissolve safely into the surrounding ocean.
Producing oxygen is only half the challenge; exhaled carbon dioxide (CO2) is toxic and will kill the crew within days if not continuously removed.
To remove carbon dioxide, the interior air is blown through liquid amine scrubbers containing monoethanolamine (MEA), which chemically binds to CO2 at room temperature.
Once saturated, the amine solution is heated inside a closed boiler, causing the amine to release the trapped CO2 gas, which is pumped overboard into the sea.
After cooling down, the amine liquid is recirculated to capture more CO2 in a continuous, indefinitely reusable closed loop.
Catalytic burner units running at over 300 degrees Celsius burn off trace contaminants like carbon monoxide from cooking and hydrogen gas off-gassing from lead-acid backup batteries.
For power-failure emergencies where electrolysis stops, submarines carry solid chemical 'oxygen candles' made of sodium chlorate and iron powder.
When struck with a mechanical primer like a road flare, an oxygen candle burns thermally, producing enough breathable oxygen for dozens of crew members for an hour.

Because reactor fuel lasts up to 25 years and air and freshwater are manufactured indefinitely, a nuclear submarine's only true limit to staying underwater is the amount of food it can physically carry.
